before.title: Authoring questions stay executable graph recipes

intent.outcome: Answer recurring maturity and verifier questions by scripting the graph rather than adding query verbs.

rules: Promotion preflight reports the Spec's stated rung, floor reached, current floor failures, and both next rungs as `aboveStated` and `aboveFloor`, each with `rung`, `failures` and `firstUnmetClause`; `rung` is null at `ready`, and a typed-dependency failure carries its targets.

before.title: The evaluation sink runs one body and prints its return

intent.problem: How `sdp q` takes a body, prints its answer and refuses is stated only in the CLI help and the reading skill, so a caller and a script that runs a recipe learn the contract by trial.
intent.outcome: State how the evaluation sink takes a body, renders its return and refuses, so every caller relies on one contract.

rules: `sdp q` takes one positional JavaScript async-function body, which takes precedence over stdin; with no positional body it reads non-terminal stdin, and absent, unreadable or empty input refuses with exit 1 before evaluation.

The sink supplies `g`, `graph`, `report` and `params`, permits `await` and prints the returned value using bounded `util.inspect` by default or `JSON.stringify` with `--json`; it does not suppress console output, so machine-consumed bodies must avoid it.

A body that returns `undefined` prints no answer, reports on stderr that `return` is the output contract and exits 0; a `--json` result with no JSON form or one that cannot be serialized refuses with exit 1 and no rendered answer.

An extraction error prevents evaluation, renders the extraction findings and exits 1; validation findings are supplied as `report` and do not gate evaluation. A compilation, evaluation or rendering failure exits 1 and reports its error on stderr.
A body that fails to parse is reported with the line and column of the error in the body the caller wrote.

design.parseErrorLine: A body that does not parse prints one stderr line, `sdp q: the body does not parse at line L, column C: <message>`, with 1-based positions in the caller's body, exits 1 and prints nothing on stdout.

before.title: The reading skill teaches agents to query the graph

intent.outcome: Give an agent a shipped reading on-ramp that selects current graph evidence and the Spec that owns each law.

rules: The skill names the closed graph node types, edge types and claims, links their carrying Specs, and moves when those contracts change.

before.title: Mermaid diagrams can be rooted at code units
before.narrative: The shipped Mermaid projection draws bounded diagrams rooted at a Spec or a Pack. A Spec-rooted diagram within the bounds includes directly bound code units and test anchors; component membership and uses are read through the census and structural recipes. A view rooted at code units could group components by their layer and context. Adding it to the shipped Mermaid root would need a decision that narrows or replaces the projection freeze. Whether it becomes a separate root or part of the Studio's architecture lens remains open.

before.title: Source anchors bind code without carrying intent

intent.outcome: Connect implementation, tests, and oracles to Specs while keeping authored intent centralized in the carrier.

terms.anchor: A human-written source binding from one code location into the graph, carrying identity, an optional label, zero or more targets, and optional structure; written in one of two extracted representations, the constant form or the comment form, which feed one closed envelope. It never carries behavior, rationale, readiness, status, acceptance criteria, or delivery facts.
terms.constant form: The top-level const initialized with a trusted builder call; the extractor reifies it statically. The decorator form remains an unextracted representation.
terms.comment form: A top-level `/** … */` block in a `.ts` or `.tsx` file carrying reserved camelCase tags (`@sdpAnchor`, `@sdpLabel`, `@sdpSatisfies`, `@sdpVerifies`, `@sdpModels`, `@sdpReferences`, `@sdpComponent`, `@sdpUses`, `@sdpRole`, `@sdpLayer`, `@sdpContext`); `@sdpAnchor <id>` opens it, each tag appears at most once, prose precedes the tags, only the reserved tags are read, and comment prose authors nothing. No import is required: trust is by reserved grammar. The same id in both forms is a duplicate id. The law is the comment-form ruling (MD-36).
terms.anchors subpath: The zero-dependency package subpath `@libar-dev/software-delivery-protocol/anchors`, exporting the id builders and the three anchor builders and nothing else; the extractor trusts it as a Protocol builder module.
terms.code anchor: An implementation-flavored binding in the `impl:`, `api:`, or `component:` namespace. Its optional, plural `satisfies` derives one anchored `satisfies` edge per target; its optional `references` derives one anchored `references` edge per target. It may also name one `component:` anchor it belongs to, a non-empty list of distinct code units it `uses`, and a `role`; a `component:` anchor may also name `layer` and `context`. The binding grain is the binding-grain ruling (MD-37); the structural attributes are the architectural-annotation ruling (MD-38).
terms.plural targets: `satisfies` on a code anchor and `verifies` on a test anchor accept one `ref(…)` or a fresh array literal of them; `verifies` is non-empty. Each resolving target confers its fact as a single target does, and `implemented` stays a whole-Spec fact.
terms.identity-only anchor: A code anchor with no `satisfies` and no `references`; it mints a CodeNode for structure and for `byFile`, derives no realization edge, and confers nothing.
terms.references: The anchored CodeNode-to-Spec edge derived from `references?: readonly SpecId[]` on a code anchor: this code answers to that design without claiming to realize it. The unit follows the design or realizes part of it, so a change to the design asks the code to follow. The direction is one way: a design that builds on existing code states that on its own side, by a `dependsOn` or `refines` relation to the Spec the code satisfies, never by a reference from the code. It confers no delivery fact, moves no readiness floor, and the drift alarm ignores it; a target also named in `satisfies` is an error. The reader reports the referencing units on the Spec's context, and blast radius traverses the edge as a binding.
terms.role: An optional one-token value on a code anchor, lowercase kebab and never normalized, naming the architectural pattern the unit plays; a corpus-owned vocabulary whose taxonomy the census renders with counts, checked against no list.
terms.layer: An optional attribute of a `component:` anchor, one of `edge`, `application`, `domain`, `adapter`, or `infrastructure`; a value outside the set, or the attribute on a non-component anchor, is an envelope error.
terms.context: An optional one-token value on a `component:` anchor, in the token grammar of a role, naming its bounded context; on a non-component anchor it is an envelope error.
terms.declared component: The `component:` anchor is the component's declaration; there is no separate architecture file, because the anchor sits where the component is realized.
terms.component realization convention: A `component:` anchor that satisfies a Spec satisfies its seam's most-specific design Spec; that `satisfies` edge is the component's own realization claim. As guidance, checked by no validator: a component either satisfies its seam's design Spec or binds no Spec its members satisfy, and it never references one. Structural edges confer nothing (the architectural-annotation ruling, MD-38).
terms.structural anchor validity: A `memberOf` source is an `impl:` or `api:` CodeNode and its target is a `component:` CodeNode; every structural target exists, every edge is unique, each source has at most one component, and structural self-reference is refused. A malformed or non-static structural field, an unknown `layer`, or `layer` or `context` on a non-component anchor refuses the whole anchor at reification; a graph-validly reified edge that later fails referential or structural validation remains visible with its anchor and independent `satisfies` binding. Multi-node `uses` cycles remain data and produce no finding.
terms.structural non-conferral: Structural edges, `role`, `layer`, and `context` carry no intent, delivery fact, readiness effect, or binding-to-Spec traversal; no `implements` field is admitted.
terms.test anchor: A binding in the `test:` namespace that derives one anchored `verifies` edge per target from a test to each Spec it verifies.
terms.oracle anchor: A binding in the `oracle:` namespace that records an oracle's `models` target without deriving a delivery fact.
terms.executable binding boundary: A resolving `specTest` anchor can establish verifier realization; a registrar activation or a `bindExample` call executes a generated contract but is not extracted graph data, so the graph cannot claim from that call alone that the contract is bound.
terms.document-realization binding: When the realizing artifact is authored Markdown that cannot carry an extracted in-code anchor, the executable suite that asserts the shipped document may carry its code anchor. Its label must name the document realization rather than imply the test body is the product, and file-level blast radius remains coverage-unknown for the Markdown artifact.
terms.Protocol builder binding: A builder import from the public Protocol package or its anchors subpath, or a relative import whose importer-relative resolution, including the TypeScript `.js`-to-`.ts` convention, canonicalizes to this package's `ids` or `model/code-anchor` module; consumer-local lookalike modules confer no binding authority. On the CommonJS package surface the trusted relative-module set is empty (`import.meta.url` is rewritten away), so relative bindings mint no anchors there while package imports stay trusted. The comment form needs no builder binding.
terms.untrusted builder: A constant-form builder call whose import is no Protocol builder binding: it mints nothing and reports nothing, because a source file that never bound to the Protocol is not authoring drift to report.

design.structuralValidator: `conformance/structural-anchors`, the conformance error for graph structural-anchor violations; referential integrity and generic edge-contract errors keep their own diagnostic ownership.

given: a repository whose one source file builds an anchor through {builderSource:"a consumer-local lookalike module"|"a relative import resolving to the Protocol builder modules"|"the published Protocol package"}

before.title: What a Spec's design carries is derived, beside its readiness
before.narrative: The original design's `designed` stage meant a Spec's key concepts were settled before code (`docs/lineage/v0-design/01-core-primitives.md` §1.4 and §8). The Protocol's readiness describes the maturity of intent. The graph therefore derives what design a Spec carries beside readiness, without adding a rung, floor clause or delivery fact. A new rung would change the locked readiness values, a floor clause reading Design would close that section's shape, and a design fact would mix design with realization signals.

intent.problem: A reviewer or an implementer cannot tell from readiness alone which Specs carry a settled design and which carry only intent, and the first adopter's owner asked for Specs whose key concepts are designed as stubs before code.
intent.outcome: Show what design a Spec carries in values the graph derives, so the backlog and a review can tell a designed Spec from one that states only its intent.
assumptions: The design columns tell a Spec with pinned declarations and keyed entries from one that states only its intent.

openQuestions.question: If the first adopter's design passes show that the design columns cannot distinguish settled design from intent alone, should this representation be revisited?
openQuestions.provisional: derive what design a Spec carries beside readiness without a new rung, floor clause or delivery fact

terms.design columns: The counts and lists the reader derives for a Spec beside its readiness under spec:consumers.pack-design; they are read on every pass and never stated.
terms.designed stage: The original design's readiness stage for a Spec whose key concepts were settled; it is not a Protocol rung.

before.title: A rule or flow entry may carry a key that addresses it
before.narrative: The original design gave a behavior rule an optional id, so the rule could later be promoted to a Spec of its own, and an optional rationale (`docs/lineage/v0-design/01-core-primitives.md` §2.2). The Protocol kept promotion and dropped the id. An unkeyed rule has no address, so a review finding, a register row or an example cannot name it; a key gives it an address. Open questions carry optional keys on the entry-address key grammar; this Spec follows that pattern for rules.

intent.problem: An inline rule has no identity but its position and its text, so anything outside the Spec that cites one rule breaks silently when the rules above it move or the rule is reworded.
intent.outcome: Let an author key a rule or flow entry, so a review, a register row or an example can name the entry it is about.

rules: Every entry of a Spec's primary behavior owner may carry an optional key on the open-question key grammar: the `rule:` and `flow:` entries of Behavior, the entries of Rule and Contract, and the entries and `rule:` entries of Workflow. One Spec keeps one key namespace across them, unique among its keyed entries, and an unkeyed entry stays lawful and has no address.

A key sits in a marker at the start of the entry's text, after the `rule:` or `flow:` label where the entry has one, as in `- rule: [#graphOnly] The Studio is a projection.` and `- [#oneFamily] Every validator belongs to one family.`, the shape an open question's marker uses, so one form serves labelled and plain entries.

Every keyed entry is addressed as `spec:<id>#rule.<key>` whatever its section, because a Spec uses one primary behavior owner. The address resolves while the Spec carries an entry with that key and fails validation in every Spec that names it once the key is renamed or removed.
A rule address is refused in every id slot, as every entry address is, so no anchor targets a rule and no delivery fact attaches to one.

An example names the keyed rules it exercises on its `verifies` relation: the target is an object with `target` and `exercises`, a list of the verified Spec's rule keys, beside an optional `reason`. A key the verified Spec does not carry is a conformance error at the relation, as a missing entry address is. The list mints no edge and confers no delivery fact, so `verifies` stays whole-Spec, and a rule-coverage recipe reads it to report which keyed rules a bound example exercises and which none does.
A keyed entry carries its key and its text and nothing else; why a rule holds is the Spec's narrative, or a decision Spec named through `decidedBy` when the why passes the ADR three-part test.
A keyed rule promoted to a Spec of its own leaves its address behind, because promotion moves the content out, and every mention of that address fails until it names the new Spec.

design.keyMarker: `[#<key>]` and one space open the entry's text, after `rule: ` or `flow: ` where the entry has a label, with the key on the open-question key grammar, `^[a-z][A-Za-z0-9]*$`; text that opens with `[#` and does not match is refused at its line, and a marker later in the text is plain text.

before.title: Declared architecture rules are checked against anchored structure
before.narrative:
The original design gave architecture a validation tier of its own. Its rules said that only adapter components depend on external systems, that domain code imports no infrastructure and that layers depend in one direction; dependency-cruiser, architecture tests and lint rules ran them, and their findings joined the one report (`docs/lineage/v0-design/06-extraction-and-validation.md` §6.4). Since the architectural annotation decision, the data those rules read is in the graph with no inference: a component anchor states its layer and its context, and `uses` and `memberOf` edges are anchored. The same decision keeps the check out of the Protocol. A negative architecture constraint stays declared intent in a Spec, and a corpus that wants it enforced checks its declared `uses`, `layer` and `context` in its own gate.

The first adopter checks that a component in its `platform` context has no `uses` edge to a component in another context, resolving each end through `memberOf`. Architecture crossings, recipe 32, reports differences in context or layer and refuses nothing. The architectural annotation decision keeps architecture checks in the corpus's own gate, and the Protocol supplies the reusable graph walk.

intent.problem: A corpus that states an architecture rule in a Spec cannot have it checked by the Protocol, so each adopter writes the same walk over `uses`, `memberOf`, `layer` and `context` in its own gate.
intent.outcome: Check a corpus's declared architecture rules, such as a forbidden uses direction or context isolation, against the layers, contexts and uses its anchors state.

openQuestions.question: Do corpus rules need to require a component to state a layer or context, or check ports and routes that anchors do not carry, beyond the selected forbidden layer pairs and isolated contexts?
openQuestions.provisional: the supplied walk checks forbidden layer pairs and isolated contexts; absent attributes are unclassified rather than breaches

openQuestions.question: Which pure callable walk serves both the catalog recipe and a loaded corpus rule, and what rule-data and result shapes do they share?
openQuestions.provisional: one pure walk takes `params.forbidden`, a list of `{ from, to }` layer pairs, and `params.isolated`, a list of context tokens whose components may have no `uses` edge into another context, either list possibly empty; it returns each forbidden edge as `{ from, to, fromComponent, toComponent, rule }` and lists unclassified edges apart; recipe 32's result stays as it is

rules: The Protocol's validators never judge a corpus's architecture; an architecture rule runs as one of the corpus's own rules, the corpus's gate decides what fails, and that gate may be the corpus's own invocation of `sdp validate --rules` with the severity the rule states.

A corpus states each architecture rule as intent in a `constraint` Spec that says what is forbidden and why, and keeps the rule's machine form, its forbidden layer pairs and isolated contexts, as data its corpus rule passes to the walk.

The Protocol supplies the walk as a catalog recipe that takes forbidden layer pairs and isolated contexts as recipe parameters, resolves each end of every anchored `uses` edge to its component, directly or through `memberOf`, and returns each edge a rule forbids with both units, both components and the rule.
The walk reads the given rules and anchored structure only; it infers no edge from imports, reads no file path, judges no role and refuses nothing.
A component that states no layer or context falls outside a rule that names one, and the walk reports it as unclassified rather than as a breach.

The corpus binds a discovered TypeScript check site to its constraint Spec through a test anchor; that check invokes the corpus rule, and `has-verifier` states that the check exists while its result stays in the corpus's run.

before.title: Corpus-authored rules run on the one validation path
before.narrative:
The original design let a team add its own rules beside the built-in validators, each with an id, a severity and the whole graph query API, run in the same pass and reported in the same output (`docs/lineage/v0-design/06-extraction-and-validation.md` §6.5). The Protocol has two check families, conformance and honesty, and every validator belongs to one of them. The architectural annotation decision sends a corpus's own rules to the corpus's own gate.

The first adopter's gate runs `sdp validate` and parses its summary line, then checks its own context isolation, entry addresses, dependency cycles, question keys, prose mentions, cited laws and Pack pages. It also parses carrier frontmatter to read kind, readiness and relations, a second read model that a graph-based corpus-rule runner would remove.

intent.problem: A corpus with rules of its own checks them off the one validation path, reading the carriers a second way and reporting in a form no Protocol surface reads.
intent.outcome: Let a corpus author its own graph rules and have their findings join the one validation report, so no corpus re-parses its carriers to check itself.

openQuestions.question: Does an operator-named rules file hold one async body returning findings or a module exporting named rule functions, how are parameters supplied, in what order do several files run, and does `sdp validate --watch` rerun them?
openQuestions.provisional: one async body per file, given `g`, `graph`, `report` and `params`, with `params` from `sdp validate --params` and `{}` without it; files run in the order named, each to completion; a rule id is unique within its file; `sdp validate --watch` runs the same named rules each cycle

openQuestions.question: What shape does a corpus finding take beside the one diagnostic currency, where does the report carry it, and does it reach `report`, the reader's `findings()` or the Design Review?
openQuestions.provisional: the shared finding contract has a Protocol branch carrying `validatorId`, `family`, severity and message, and a corpus branch carrying the corpus, the rule id as `validatorId`, `subjectId`, severity and message and no family; `relatedId`, `path`, `file` and `line` stay optional on both branches; corpus findings are collected as `corpusFindings` in the same report and rendered under a corpus-labelled section with the existing location, severity, identifier and message composition; Protocol findings, the summary line and the Design Review stay unchanged, as the frozen-projections decision requires

openQuestions.question: Does the runner enforce that a rule reads only the graph and changes nothing, or are both obligations on the rule's author?
openQuestions.provisional: changing nothing is a guarantee, with the Protocol's validators run first and each rule given a frozen or cloned graph; reading only the graph is the author's obligation, run with the trust `sdp q` asks and no sandbox

rules: A corpus rule is a graph body the corpus authors, given `g`, `graph`, `report` and `params` as a recipe body is, and returning findings that each carry a rule id, a subject, a message and a severity.
A corpus rule reads the one derived graph and nothing else, so no rule reads a carrier, a source file or the network.
Each corpus finding names its rule and its corpus as its source and stands apart from the Protocol's own findings; the Protocol states none of these rules and ships none.

Corpus findings stand outside the conformance and honesty families, in a section of the report labelled as the corpus's own, so the two families keep their meaning and the guardrail that checks never judge content quality or workflow keeps binding the Protocol's own validators.

Validation runs corpus rules only from a file the operator names with `sdp validate --rules PATH`, which may repeat, and never from a file it finds in the corpus or in a configuration; it asks the trust `sdp q` already asks, to run code the operator chose.

A corpus finding carries severity `error` or `warning`. When the operator names `--rules`, an `error` corpus finding makes `sdp validate` exit nonzero and a `warning` stays informative; without `--rules` no corpus rule runs and only the Protocol's validators set the exit code.
Corpus findings keep their own source and report section, are tallied apart from the Protocol's summary line, and neither add to, suppress nor change a Protocol finding or the exit reason it sets.

A rules file that cannot load, a rule that throws, or a rule that returns a finding without a rule id, subject, message and admitted severity is a rule execution failure; `sdp validate` reports it in the corpus section and exits nonzero, so a broken rule never passes as a clean run.
A corpus rule changes no node, edge or delivery fact; it reports on the graph it is given.
